headline: Sakebi is the continuative stem of the verb 叫ぶ (sakebu, “to scream, to shout, to cry”).
In yokubō, 欲 is a daiyōji replacing 慾.
Kyōzon is, by surface analysis, 共 (kyō, “co-”) plus 存 (zon, “exist”).
Tsuba appears to be a shortening of tsubaki, or perhaps a fusion of tsu with the particle は.
Kusa, “grass”, is from Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *kusa, and is found in the Man'yōshū.
Heihō is probably from Chinese 平方 (píngfāng, literally “flat square”), first attested in Japanese in 1875.
ポンプ is borrowed from Dutch pomp.
Dekai is generally considered a variation of どいかい (doikai), from the emphasizing prefix ど (do-, “very”) plus 厳い (ikai, “great, huge, many”), though one dictionary disputes the sound change.
Omake is 御 (o-, honorific prefix) plus 負け (make), the stem of 負ける (makeru, “to lower in price”).
Inori is the continuative stem of the verb 祈る (inoru, “to pray”).
ガイドブック is from English guidebook.
Jiten is 自 (ji, “self”) plus 転 (ten, “rotate; round”).
Kaigara is 貝 (kai, “shellfish”) plus 殻 (kara, “shell”), with kara voiced to gara by rendaku.
エンジニア is borrowed from English engineer.
Renkyū is 連 (ren, “consecutive”) plus 休 (kyū, “day off”).
ゲーム is borrowed from English game.
サンタクロース is borrowed from English Santa Claus.
Sanmyaku is from Middle Chinese 山脈 (MC srean meak).
Shimatsu may be a Japanese coinage from Middle Chinese-derived parts, 始 (shi, “beginning”) plus 末 (matsu, “end”).
Hina appears to be from Old Japanese; a derived form, hiwina, appears in The Tale of Genji, dated before 1021.
Marumeru is from Old Japanese 丸む (marumu), a lower bigrade verb that became a lower monograde one.
San, “acid”, is from Middle Chinese 酸 (swan).
Kōkogaku is 考古 (kōko, “archaeology”) plus 学 (-gaku, “study”).
シート covers “seat” and “sheet”, and the source borrows both from English.
ジャンプ is borrowed from English jump.
Tanso is 炭 (tan, “coal”) plus 素 (so, “element”), a calque of Dutch koolstof coined by Udagawa Yōan in 1834.
Yōsei is from the Middle Chinese compound 要請, literally “demand + request”.
ジャンボ is borrowed from English jumbo.
Azamuku is a shift from 浅向く (asamuku).
Hiritsu is 比 (hi, “ratio”) plus 率 (ritsu, “rate”).
Chōshū is 徴 (chō, “collect taxes or payment”) plus 収 (shū, “collect”).
